text:
Beetroot.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Beetroot’s sweet, earthy roots suit raw salads, hot dishes, pickles, borsch and chutneys; young leaves are edible too. This cool-climate crop needs well-drained, humus-rich soil and steady moisture. Growth starts slowly, then roots swell quickly. Sow small batches for summer, autumn and storage crops. Lift before roots become woody or leathery. In mild winters some can stay outside, but severe frost can freeze and rot them.

Quick facts
Sow

Apr – Jun

Harvest

Jun – Nov

Germination

10–14 days

Sowing depth

1 in.

Row spacing

12 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

globe: 10 lb; long: 18 lb

Plant spacing

4 in. between plants

Ready in

From sowing: globe roots ~11 weeks; long roots ~16 weeks

Later sowings

Sow late May–Jul for storage.

GLOBE · RED
Boltardy

A familiar round red beetroot valued for resistance to bolting. A useful choice for earlier sowings under suitable conditions.

GLOBE · RED

A round red beetroot producing uniform roots with good kitchen quality. Harvest young for tender roots.

CYLINDRICAL

Long, cylindrical red roots make even slices easy. Useful for cooking and pickling when shape matters more than round presentation.

GLOBE · RED

A heritage beetroot with pink-and-white rings when cut raw. Grow for visual variety alongside a standard red beetroot.

CYLINDRICAL

An elongated red beetroot with a tidy shape for slicing. Retain as an established alternative to round-rooted selections.

GLOBE · RED
Red Ace F1

F1 hybrid with round roots and dark red flesh.

Key risks
Bolting

Plants sometimes run to seed before roots have developed.

Fanging

Forked roots are usually caused by adding fresh manure shortly before sowing.

Mangold fly (leaf miner)

Small white grubs burrow inside the leaves, causing tunnels which later turn into blisters.

Heart rot

Leaves wilt in summer and the tops of the roots develop brown, sunken patches.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
26
ROOT CROPS

A cool-climate crop.

Use well-drained soil rich in organic matter.

Keep moisture steady.

Drought hardens roots; sudden wet can split them.

Sow for a long season.

Successive sowings extend the harvest.

Soil & preparation
Use humus-rich, well-drained soil without fresh manure. Remove stones; long roots need deep, sandy ground.
Use previously manured ground or add autumn compost. Lime acid soil towards pH 6.5; feed poor ground if needed.
Sowing & planting
Sow seed clusters
Thin seedlings
Sow 

Place two seed clusters every 4 in., 1 in. deep, in rows 12 in. apart. Keep the seedbed moist. Soaking the clusters for a few hours or overnight can help germination.

Looking after the crop
Each seed cluster can produce several seedlings. When they are 1 in. high, thin to one plant at each spot. Protect them from birds.
Hoe gently. Mulch and water evenly. Drought makes roots woody and a sudden soaking can split them.
Fleece can bring the crop forward. Weed beneath it regularly. Pick young leaves to use like spinach.
Harvesting & storage
Pull globe roots before they reach cricket-ball size.
Fork up storage roots in autumn without piercing them. Twist off the leaves, leaving short stalks.
In mild winters roots can stay in the ground. Lift before severe frost. Pack sound roots apart in paper sacks or moist sand and keep cool.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting	Early flowering; poor roots.	Avoid early sowing; thin promptly; use resistant varieties.
Fanging	Forked roots.	Avoid fresh manure and stones; prepare soil well.
Mangold fly (leaf miner)	Blisters and tunnels in leaves.	Crush larvae in mines; use mesh on a rotated bed.
Heart rot	Brown or black areas inside roots.	Confirm boron shortage; seek organic correction advice.
Blackleg	Seedlings blacken and collapse.	Remove affected seedlings; improve drainage.
Speckled yellows	Yellow patches; rolled edges.	Confirm manganese shortage; avoid excess lime.
Autumnal fungal root rots	Dark rot in wet autumns.	Lift promptly; store only sound roots.
Leaf spot	Brown spots with pale centres.	Remove badly affected leaves; rotate; add compost.
Final tips

Twist off foliage; do not cut roots for storage.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 104–105 · Growing Techniques 150
